variants.question: What term describes a well-defined collection of distinct objects?
What is each object inside a set called?
variants.answer: An element (or member) of the set

variants.question: What is a set with no elements called?
What is a set with exactly one element called?

distractorPool: An element (or member) of the set
se_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Set language is built from a small number of precise terms — a set, its elements, and special cases like the empty set (zero elements) and a singleton set (exactly one element) — each describing a distinct, well-defined idea.
se_l1_t1.realPurpose: This vocabulary is the foundation for all of set theory, which underlies how databases, search engines and even Venn-diagram-style reasoning organise and compare groups of items.

variants.question: Two sets that contain exactly the same elements are called:
Two sets that have the same number of elements, but not necessarily the same elements, are called:
A set that contains every element under consideration in a particular context is called:

se_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Equal sets require identical elements, equivalent sets only require a matching element count, and a universal set is simply the agreed 'everything' being considered — three distinct relationships that are easy to confuse without precise definitions.
se_l1_t2.realPurpose: This precision matters because mixing up 'equal' and 'equivalent' is one of the most common set-theory misconceptions, despite the two ideas being quite different.

variants.question: Writing a set by listing all of its elements, such as {2, 4, 6, 8}, is called:
Writing a set by describing a property its elements share, such as 'the set of all even numbers less than 10', is called:

se_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Roster form lists every element explicitly, which works well for small, finite sets, while set-builder form describes a shared property, which is essential for large or infinite sets that can't practically be listed one by one.
se_l1_t3.realPurpose: Choosing the right notation matters in practice — set-builder form is what allows mathematicians to precisely describe sets like 'all even numbers,' which would be impossible to fully list.

variants.question: What is the term for a diagram that uses overlapping circles inside a rectangle to represent sets and their relationships?
The set containing all elements that are in either of two sets (or both) is called their:
The set containing only the elements that are common to both sets is called their:

se_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Venn diagrams give union and intersection a visual meaning: union is everything covered by either circle, while intersection is only the overlapping region shared by both circles.
se_l1_t4.realPurpose: Union and intersection are used constantly in real life, from search engines combining or narrowing results to databases filtering records that meet one or multiple conditions.

se_l2_t1.questionTemplate: Set A = {{{elementsDisplay}}}. How many elements does Set A contain? (This is written as n(A).)
se_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: The number of elements in a set, called its cardinality and written n(A), is found simply by counting each distinct element exactly once.
se_l2_t1.realPurpose: Cardinality notation lets mathematicians refer to the 'size' of a set precisely and compactly, without needing to list out every element each time.

se_l2_t2.questionTemplate: Set A has {{countA}} elements and Set B has {{countB}} elements, with no elements in common between them. How many elements are in the union of A and B (A ∪ B)?
se_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: When two sets share no common elements (called disjoint sets), the union simply combines every element from both sets, so its size is exactly the sum of the two individual sizes.
se_l2_t2.realPurpose: This special case (disjoint sets) is the simplest form of the general union rule, which must be adjusted whenever sets do overlap.

se_l2_t3.questionTemplate: Set A has {{countA}} elements and Set B has {{countB}} elements. If {{overlap}} elements are common to both sets, how many elements are in A ∪ B (the union)? (Use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B))
se_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Whenever two sets overlap, simply adding their sizes counts the shared elements twice, so the overlap (intersection) must be subtracted once to get the correct total union size.
se_l2_t3.realPurpose: This formula is used whenever real overlapping groups need to be combined accurately, such as counting students enrolled in at least one of two different clubs.

se_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A set contains {{n}} elements. Using the formula (Number of subsets = 2ⁿ), how many total subsets does this set have, including the empty set and the set itself?
se_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Each element in a set has exactly two possibilities when forming a subset — either it's included or it isn't — so multiplying these two choices together for every element gives 2 raised to the power of the total number of elements.
se_l2_t4.realPurpose: This doubling pattern shows why the number of possible subsets grows extremely quickly as a set gets larger, a concept closely related to counting possible combinations in probability.

variants.question: A student lists {2, 2, 3, 4} as a valid set with 4 elements, not realising sets don't count repeated elements separately. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Sets only contain DISTINCT elements; repeating an element doesn't add it again, so {2, 2, 3, 4} is actually the same as {2, 3, 4}, a set with only 3 elements, not 4
distractors: The student is correct — repeated elements are counted separately, so {2, 2, 3, 4} genuinely has 4 elements
The set {2, 2, 3, 4} is invalid and cannot be written this way under any circumstances
Repeated elements double the 'weight' of that element without changing the total element count

se_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: A defining property of a set is that its elements are distinct — writing an element more than once doesn't create a second copy within the set, it simply refers to the same single element again.
se_l3_t1.realPurpose: This distinctness rule is exactly why sets are useful for representing unique collections, such as a list of unique visitors to a website, without accidentally double-counting repeats.

variants.question: A student assumes the empty set has zero subsets, reasoning that 'there's nothing inside it to make subsets from.' What is the mistake?
variants.answer: The empty set actually has exactly ONE subset — itself (the empty set is considered a subset of every set, including itself); using the 2ⁿ formula with n = 0 gives 2⁰ = 1, confirming this
distractors: The student is correct — the empty set has zero subsets, since there are no elements to form any subsets from
The empty set has an undefined number of subsets, since the formula 2ⁿ does not apply to it
The empty set has exactly 2 subsets, matching the smallest non-empty set

se_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: The subset-counting formula 2ⁿ works even when n = 0, since any number raised to the power 0 equals 1; this single subset is the empty set itself, which is defined to be a subset of every set, including itself.
se_l3_t2.realPurpose: Recognising this edge case correctly is important for applying the 2ⁿ subset formula consistently, without treating the empty set as a special exception.

variants.question: A student assumes two sets with the same NUMBER of elements must always be equal sets. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Having the same number of elements only makes two sets EQUIVALENT, not necessarily EQUAL; equal sets must contain the exact same elements, while equivalent sets just need matching sizes (e.g., {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5, 6} are equivalent but not equal)
distractors: The student is correct — any two sets with the same number of elements must always be equal sets
Equal sets and equivalent sets are simply two different names for the exact same relationship
Two sets can only be equivalent if they are also equal, since equivalence requires identical elements

se_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Equality between sets is a stricter requirement than equivalence: equal sets must match element-for-element, while equivalent sets only need to match in total count, regardless of what those elements actually are.
se_l3_t3.realPurpose: This distinction prevents a common mix-up and reinforces that 'same size' and 'same contents' are genuinely different mathematical relationships.

variants.question: A student adds n(A) and n(B) directly to find n(A ∪ B), even when the two sets overlap, without subtracting the intersection. What is the mistake in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Whenever two sets share common elements, simply adding n(A) + n(B) counts the shared (overlapping) elements TWICE; the correct formula n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) subtracts the overlap once to correct for this double-counting
distractors: The student is correct — n(A ∪ B) is always found by simply adding n(A) and n(B), even when the sets overlap
Overlapping elements should be counted three times to properly account for the overlap
The union formula only applies to sets that do NOT overlap; overlapping sets have no defined union

se_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: This is the same double-counting error the union formula is specifically designed to correct — overlapping elements belong to both n(A) and n(B), so a plain sum counts them twice unless the intersection is subtracted back out once.
se_l3_t4.realPurpose: Recognising this error reinforces exactly why the subtract-the-overlap step in the union formula is necessary, not optional.

variants.question: Which is the smallest number system that the number 7 belongs to?
Which is the smallest number system that the number 0 belongs to?
Which is the smallest number system that the number −5 belongs to?

int_l1_split.technicalIntricacy: The number systems are nested inside one another (Natural Numbers ⊂ Whole Numbers ⊂ Integers ⊂ Rational Numbers), so identifying the smallest system a number belongs to means finding the most restrictive category it still fits into.
int_l1_split.realPurpose: Understanding these nested categories clarifies why every natural number is automatically also a whole number and an integer, but not the other way around.

variants.question: What is the absolute value of −7?
Which integer is greater: −3 or −8?
What is the additive inverse (opposite) of 9?

int_l1_new.technicalIntricacy: Absolute value measures an integer's distance from zero regardless of sign; comparing negative integers works in the opposite direction to their size (−3 is greater than −8, since it is closer to zero); and the additive inverse of any integer is the same number with its sign flipped.
int_l1_new.realPurpose: These integer skills apply whenever real-world quantities involve direction or deficit, such as temperatures below zero, elevations below sea level, or a bank account overdraft.

int_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: Adding a negative integer moves further down the number line, while adding a positive integer moves up; the sum's sign depends on which of the two integers has the greater absolute value.
int_l2_new1.realPurpose: Integer addition models real combined changes, such as a temperature rising and then falling, or a bank balance after a deposit and a withdrawal.

int_l2_new2.technicalIntricacy: Subtracting an integer is the same as adding its additive inverse, so subtracting a negative number actually increases the result — a point that trips up many students first learning integer subtraction.
int_l2_new2.realPurpose: This rule is essential for correctly calculating differences involving negative values, such as the temperature change between −5°C and 10°C.

variants.question: A student simplifies 8 − (−5) as 3, treating the two minus signs as cancelling to leave just a subtraction. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its positive counterpart, so 8 − (−5) = 8 + 5 = 13, not 3; the two negative signs combine to flip the operation to addition, not disappear entirely
distractors: The student's method is correct, since two negative signs always disappear entirely, leaving 8 − 5 = 3
Subtracting a negative always gives a negative result, so 8 − (−5) = −13
The expression is undefined because you cannot subtract a negative number

int_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: Subtracting a number is defined as adding its additive inverse; since the additive inverse of −5 is +5, subtracting −5 is identical to adding 5, not to a plain subtraction of two positive fives.
int_l3_new1.realPurpose: This exact rule is why double-negative expressions appear throughout algebra, and misapplying it is one of the most common integer-arithmetic mistakes.

variants.question: A student believes (−4) × (−6) equals −24, since 'a negative times anything should stay negative.' What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Multiplying two negative numbers always produces a POSITIVE result, so (−4) × (−6) = 24, not −24; the two negative signs cancel out during multiplication (unlike addition, where they don't)
distractors: The student is correct — two negative numbers multiplied together always give a negative result
The result should be 0, since negative numbers multiplied together cancel out completely
The sign of the result depends on which number is listed first in the multiplication

int_l3_new2.technicalIntricacy: The sign rules for multiplication are fixed: positive × positive = positive, negative × negative = positive, and positive × negative (in either order) = negative — a negative result only ever comes from multiplying exactly one negative number.
int_l3_new2.realPurpose: These sign rules must be applied correctly and consistently throughout algebra, since a single sign error can flip the entire meaning of a calculated result.

variants.question: Which is the smallest number system that the number 3/4 belongs to?
Which is the smallest number system that the number −2/3 belongs to?

rat_l1_split.technicalIntricacy: A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction p/q of two integers (with q not zero); fractions that are not whole numbers only fit into this outermost category, not any of the more restrictive ones.
rat_l1_split.realPurpose: Recognising that a value like 3/4 belongs only to the rational numbers (not the narrower integer, whole, or natural categories) clarifies exactly why fractions needed their own, broader number system.

variants.question: What is the result of adding a positive rational number and its exact negative (additive inverse), such as 5/2 and −5/2?
What is the result of multiplying any rational number by 1 (the multiplicative identity)?
What is the result of multiplying any rational number by 0?

distractorPool: A negative version of the number
nm_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: These are fundamental properties of the rational number system: adding a number to its additive inverse always cancels to zero, multiplying by the identity element 1 leaves a number unchanged, and multiplying by zero collapses any number to zero.
nm_l1_t3.realPurpose: These basic rules are used constantly, often without conscious thought, whenever simplifying or checking arithmetic and algebraic expressions involving fractions.

variants.question: What is {{p}}/{{q}} + {{r}}/{{q}}, expressed as a single fraction (do not simplify)?

rat_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: When two fractions share the same denominator, they can be added by simply adding their numerators and keeping the denominator unchanged, since both fractions are already split into equal-sized parts.
rat_l2_new1.realPurpose: This same-denominator shortcut is the starting point for all fraction addition, and understanding why the denominator stays fixed is essential before tackling fractions with different denominators.

variants.question: Which rational number is equivalent to {{p}}/{{q}}?

rat_l2_new2.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying both the numerator and denominator of a fraction by the same non-zero number always produces an equivalent fraction, since the overall proportion between them stays exactly the same.
rat_l2_new2.realPurpose: Recognising equivalent fractions is essential for comparing, adding, and simplifying rational numbers, since the same value can be written in infinitely many equivalent forms.

variants.question: A student says 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5, adding the numerators together and the denominators together directly. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Fractions with different denominators cannot be added by simply adding numerators and denominators separately; they must first be converted to a common (equivalent) denominator — the correct sum is 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, not 2/5
distractors: The student's method is correct, since adding numerators and denominators directly always works for any two fractions
1/2 + 1/3 should instead be found by multiplying the two fractions together
The two fractions cannot be added at all unless they already share the same denominator

rat_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: Adding fractions requires a common denominator so that both fractions are expressed in equal-sized parts before their numerators can be meaningfully combined; adding denominators directly (as in the student's mistake) produces a fraction with no consistent mathematical meaning.
rat_l3_new1.realPurpose: This is one of the most common fraction mistakes, and avoiding it is essential before any correct fraction addition or subtraction can be performed.

variants.question: A student assumes that because 3/4 is a fraction, it cannot also be called a rational number. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Every fraction formed by dividing one integer by another non-zero integer IS, by definition, a rational number; 'fraction' and 'rational number' are not separate, unrelated categories — a fraction like 3/4 is simply one common way of writing a rational number
distractors: The student is correct — fractions and rational numbers are two entirely separate, unrelated number systems
A fraction only becomes a rational number once it is converted into a decimal
Rational numbers can only be written as whole numbers, never as fractions

rat_l3_new2.technicalIntricacy: A rational number is formally defined as any number expressible as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero; this definition directly describes what a fraction already is, so every fraction is automatically a rational number.
rat_l3_new2.realPurpose: Clarifying this relationship prevents students from treating 'fractions' and 'rational numbers' as two different topics, when fractions are simply the most familiar representation of rational numbers.

variants.question: In the fraction 5/8, what is the number 5 called?
In the fraction 5/8, what is the number 8 called?
A fraction where the numerator is smaller than the denominator, such as 3/7, is called a:
A fraction where the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator, such as 9/4, is called a:

frac_l1_new1.technicalIntricacy: A fraction's numerator (top) counts how many equal parts are taken, while its denominator (bottom) shows how many equal parts the whole was divided into; whether the numerator is smaller or larger than the denominator determines if the fraction is proper or improper.
frac_l1_new1.realPurpose: This vocabulary is essential for describing and comparing fractions precisely, and for converting confidently between improper fractions and mixed numbers.

variants.question: What mixed number is equivalent to the improper fraction 7/2?
What mixed number is equivalent to the improper fraction 11/4?
What improper fraction is equivalent to the mixed number 2⅓?

frac_l1_new2.technicalIntricacy: Converting an improper fraction to a mixed number means dividing the numerator by the denominator to find the whole-number part, with the remainder becoming the new fraction part over the same denominator — the reverse process multiplies the whole number by the denominator and adds the numerator.
frac_l1_new2.realPurpose: Mixed numbers are often easier to picture in everyday contexts (like 3½ pizzas), while improper fractions are usually easier to use in further calculations, so converting confidently between the two is an essential practical skill.

variants.question: What is {{p1}}/{{q1}} × {{p2}}/{{q2}}, expressed as a single fraction (do not simplify)?

frac_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying two fractions means multiplying their numerators together to get the new numerator, and multiplying their denominators together to get the new denominator, without needing a common denominator first.
frac_l2_new1.realPurpose: Fraction multiplication is used whenever finding 'a fraction of a fraction,' such as calculating a discount rate applied to an already-discounted price.

variants.question: What is {{p1}}/{{q1}} ÷ {{p2}}/{{q2}}, expressed as a single fraction (do not simplify)? (Hint: multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction.)

frac_l2_new2.technicalIntricacy: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (the fraction flipped upside down), because dividing by a value and multiplying by its reciprocal always produce the identical result.
frac_l2_new2.realPurpose: This 'flip and multiply' rule is essential for solving real problems like figuring out how many ¾-cup servings fit inside 6 cups of a recipe.

variants.question: A student simplifies 2/3 + 1/3 as 3/6, adding both the numerators and the denominators together. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: When two fractions already share the same denominator, only the numerators should be added, keeping the shared denominator unchanged; the correct sum is 2/3 + 1/3 = 3/3 = 1, not 3/6
distractors: The student's method is correct, since adding denominators together always keeps the fraction accurate
3/6 is correct because it simplifies to 1/2, which is close enough to the right answer
Fractions with the same denominator cannot be added at all

frac_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: The denominator represents the size of the equal parts being counted; since both fractions here are already split into thirds, adding the numerators simply counts up how many thirds there are in total, while the denominator itself never needs to change.
frac_l3_new1.realPurpose: This is a foundational fraction-addition rule, and confusing it with the different-denominator case (where a common denominator must first be found) is one of the most frequent early fraction mistakes.

variants.question: A student simplifies 16/64 by cancelling the digit '6' that appears in both the numerator and the denominator, getting 1/4, and claims this is correct because '1/4 happens to equal 16/64.' What is the flaw in this method, even though the final answer is coincidentally correct?
variants.answer: Cancelling digits that merely LOOK the same (like the '6' in 16 and 64) is not a valid simplification method — correct simplification requires dividing both the numerator and denominator by an actual common factor (here, dividing both by 16); this digit-cancelling trick only appears to work by pure coincidence and gives wrong answers on almost every other fraction
distractors: The student's method is entirely valid, since cancelling any matching digit from the numerator and denominator always works
The method is invalid because 16/64 cannot be simplified at all
The correct simplification requires cancelling the '1' in 16, not the '6'

frac_l3_new2.technicalIntricacy: Valid fraction simplification always divides both the numerator and denominator by a shared factor of the whole numbers involved; treating individual digits as cancellable regardless of their actual place value or mathematical role is a coincidental trick, not a reliable rule.
frac_l3_new2.realPurpose: Recognising why 'digit cancelling' is invalid (despite occasionally producing a correct-looking answer) reinforces what fraction simplification actually means, preventing a seductive but incorrect shortcut from taking hold.

variants.question: What is the place value of the digit 7 in the decimal number 3.75?
What is the place value of the digit 5 in the decimal number 3.75?
A decimal number whose digits after the decimal point eventually stop (like 0.25) is called a:
A decimal number whose digits after the decimal point repeat forever (like 0.333...) is called a:

dec_l1_new1.technicalIntricacy: Each position after the decimal point represents a place value ten times smaller than the one before it (tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths), and decimals are further classified by whether their digits eventually stop (terminating) or repeat forever in a pattern (recurring).
dec_l1_new1.realPurpose: Understanding decimal place value is essential for correctly reading, comparing and rounding decimal numbers, from prices in a shop to measurements in a science lab.

variants.question: Which decimal is greater: 0.45 or 0.5?
Which decimal is greater: 0.7 or 0.65?
What is 3.847 rounded to two decimal places?

dec_l1_new2.technicalIntricacy: Comparing decimals requires comparing place value by place value from left to right (not simply counting digits), and rounding to a given decimal place depends only on the very next digit after that place.
dec_l1_new2.realPurpose: These skills are used constantly in real life, from comparing prices at a shop to rounding measurements to a sensible level of precision.

dec_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: Adding decimals requires lining up the decimal points (matching each place value column) before adding, exactly as whole numbers are lined up by their place value columns.
dec_l2_new1.realPurpose: Decimal addition is used every time amounts of money, measurements, or scientific readings need to be combined accurately.

dec_l2_new2.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying a decimal by 10, 100 or 1000 simply shifts every digit's place value to the left by one, two, or three positions respectively, which visually looks like moving the decimal point the same number of places to the right.
dec_l2_new2.realPurpose: This place-value shifting shortcut is used constantly for quick mental conversions, such as between metres and millimetres, or rupees and paise.

variants.question: A student says 0.4 is smaller than 0.25, since '4 is smaller than 25 in normal counting.' What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Comparing decimals by treating the digits after the point as if they were plain whole numbers ignores place value; 0.4 means 4 tenths (equivalent to 0.40), which is larger than 0.25 (25 hundredths), because tenths represent a bigger place value than hundredths
distractors: The student is correct — 0.4 is smaller than 0.25 because 4 is a smaller digit than 25
The two decimals are exactly equal in value
Decimals with fewer digits after the point are always the smallest, regardless of place value

dec_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: Every decimal can be compared fairly by padding it with trailing zeros to the same number of decimal places first (0.4 becomes 0.40), which reveals that 0.40 is indeed greater than 0.25 when compared place by place.
dec_l3_new1.realPurpose: Avoiding this 'longer digit string means bigger number' mistake is essential for correctly ordering prices, measurements, and any decimal data.

variants.question: A student rounds 2.449 to one decimal place by first rounding to two decimal places (2.45) and then rounding that result to one decimal place (2.5). What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Rounding in multiple successive steps can produce a different (and less accurate) result than rounding directly from the original number; rounding 2.449 directly to one decimal place gives 2.4 (since the second decimal digit, 4, rounds down), not 2.5, which only appears because of the incorrect intermediate rounding step
distractors: The student's method is correct, since rounding step by step always gives the same result as rounding directly
2.449 should round to 2.0, since decimals below 2.5 always round down to the nearest whole number
Rounding decimals more than once always produces a more accurate result, not a less accurate one

dec_l3_new2.technicalIntricacy: Correct rounding always looks only at the single digit immediately after the desired rounding place in the ORIGINAL number; rounding in stages can introduce a compounding error, sometimes flipping the final digit in the wrong direction, as seen here.
dec_l3_new2.realPurpose: Avoiding double-rounding errors is important in any field requiring precise reported values, from financial calculations to scientific measurements.

variants.question: According to the laws of exponents, a<sup>m</sup> × a<sup>n</sup> equals:
According to the laws of exponents, a<sup>m</sup> ÷ a<sup>n</sup> equals:
According to the laws of exponents, (a<sup>m</sup>)<sup>n</sup> equals:

nm_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Each law of exponents follows directly from what a power actually means (repeated multiplication): multiplying same-base powers adds their exponents because you're combining two repeated-multiplication chains, while raising a power to another power multiplies the exponents because the outer power repeats the whole inner chain.
nm_l1_t2.realPurpose: The laws of exponents let mathematicians and scientists simplify extremely large or small expressions (like those in scientific notation) without expanding every multiplication by hand.

variants.question: Is 16 a perfect square, a perfect cube, or both?
Is 27 a perfect square, a perfect cube, or both?
Is 64 a perfect square, a perfect cube, or both?
variants.answer: Both a perfect square (8²) and a perfect cube (4³)

variants.question: Is 25 a perfect square, a perfect cube, or both?

distractorPool: Both a perfect square (8²) and a perfect cube (4³)
Neither a perfect square nor a perfect cube
nm_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: A perfect square is a whole number obtained by squaring another whole number, and a perfect cube is one obtained by cubing another whole number; a small number of values, like 64, happen to be both, since 64 = 8² and also 64 = 4³.
nm_l1_t4.realPurpose: Recognising perfect squares and cubes quickly speeds up finding square roots and cube roots without needing a calculator.

nm_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself exactly once more, written using the exponent 2; this is different from doubling the number (multiplying by 2), a common point of confusion.
nm_l2_t1.realPurpose: Squares are used constantly in geometry (area of a square), physics (energy and distance formulas), and statistics, making rapid, accurate squaring an essential skill.

nm_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Cubing a number means multiplying it by itself twice more (three factors in total), written using the exponent 3, which grows values much faster than squaring as the base increases.
nm_l2_t2.realPurpose: Cubes are used to calculate the volume of cube-shaped objects and appear throughout algebra and geometry wherever three-dimensional scaling is involved.

nm_l2_t3.questionTemplate: What is the square root of {{square}}?
nm_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Finding a square root means identifying which number, when multiplied by itself, produces the given value — the reverse operation of squaring.
nm_l2_t3.realPurpose: Square roots are used to find the side length of a square from its area, and appear throughout geometry, physics and statistics.

nm_l2_t4.questionTemplate: What is the cube root of {{cube}}?
nm_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: Finding a cube root means identifying which number, when multiplied by itself twice more (three factors total), produces the given value — the reverse operation of cubing.
nm_l2_t4.realPurpose: Cube roots are used to find the side length of a cube from its volume, an operation used in engineering and packaging design.

variants.question: A student simplifies a<sup>{{m}}</sup> × a<sup>{{n}}</sup> as a<sup>{{wrongResult}}</sup>, multiplying the two exponents together. What is the mistake, and what is the correct simplification?
variants.answer: a<sup>{{correctResult}}</sup>, since the exponents are added (not multiplied) when multiplying powers with the same base
distractors: a<sup>{{wrongResult}}</sup> is correct, since exponents are always multiplied when combining powers
a<sup>{{m}}</sup>, since only the larger exponent is kept
a<sup>{{n}}</sup>, since only the smaller exponent is kept

nm_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: a<sup>m</sup> × a<sup>n</sup> means (a multiplied by itself m times) multiplied by (a multiplied by itself n times), which together is a multiplied by itself (m + n) times — so the exponents must be added, not multiplied; multiplying exponents is only correct for the separate rule (a<sup>m</sup>)<sup>n</sup> = a<sup>mn</sup>.
nm_l3_t1.realPurpose: Mixing up the product-of-powers rule with the power-of-a-power rule is one of the most common exponent mistakes, so recognising the difference is essential for simplifying algebraic expressions correctly.

variants.question: A student says that (−{{base}})<sup>2</sup> equals −{{correctValue}}, reasoning that "a negative number squared should stay negative." What is the mistake, and what is the correct value?
variants.answer: {{correctValue}}, because squaring multiplies the negative number by itself, and a negative number multiplied by a negative number gives a positive result
distractors: −{{correctValue}}, because a negative number squared should stay negative
