variants.question: An isosceles triangle has a vertex (apex) angle of {{apex}}°. Since the two base angles of an isosceles triangle are always equal, what is the measure of EACH base angle?

tri_l2_new.technicalIntricacy: Since all three angles sum to 180° and the two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, subtracting the apex angle from 180° and dividing the remainder by two gives the measure of each base angle.
tri_l2_new.realPurpose: This calculation combines the triangle angle-sum property with the isosceles triangle's equal-base-angles property, a very common combination in geometry problems.

variants.question: A triangle has two interior opposite (remote) angles measuring {{remote1}}° and {{remote2}}°. A student calculates the triangle's exterior angle by adding all three interior angles together, arriving at 180°. What is the mistake, and what is the correct exterior angle?
variants.answer: {{correctExterior}}°, found by adding only the two interior opposite (remote) angles, not all three interior angles
distractors: 180°, since the exterior angle always equals the sum of all three interior angles of the triangle
{{supplementExterior}}°, since the exterior angle is the supplement of the sum of the two remote angles
Only the larger of the two remote angles determines the exterior angle

ge_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: The exterior angle property states that an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of only its two interior opposite (remote) angles, while the sum of all three interior angles is always 180° regardless of the triangle's shape, making that number meaningless as an exterior angle.
ge_l3_t1.realPurpose: This property provides a shortcut for finding exterior angles without needing to know or calculate the third interior angle first.

variants.question: A triangle has two known interior angles of {{angle1}}° and {{angle2}}°. A student calculates the third angle by subtracting only {{angle1}}° from 180°, forgetting to also subtract {{angle2}}°. What is the mistake, and what is the correct third angle?
variants.answer: {{correctThird}}°, found by subtracting BOTH known angles ({{angle1}}° and {{angle2}}°) from 180°
distractors: {{wrongThird}}°, found by subtracting only one of the two known angles from 180°
The sum of the two known angles, found by simply adding {{angle1}}° and {{angle2}}° together
The third angle cannot be found without directly measuring it

ge_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Because all three interior angles of a triangle must add up to exactly 180°, finding an unknown angle requires subtracting BOTH of the other two known angles from 180°, not just one of them.
ge_l3_t3.realPurpose: This is a common careless error when applying the angle sum property, and checking that all three final angles actually add up to 180° is a reliable way to catch this mistake.

variants.question: Triangle PQR is congruent to Triangle XYZ, with the correspondence P↔X, Q↔Y, R↔Z. If PQ = {{a}} cm, what is the length of XY?
distractors: Cannot be determined without more information

cong_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: Congruent triangles have exactly equal corresponding sides and angles, so any side in one triangle is automatically equal in length to its corresponding side in the other triangle.
cong_l2_new1.realPurpose: This direct correspondence is what makes congruence so useful in manufacturing and design — confirming two parts are congruent instantly confirms every one of their matching measurements is identical.

variants.question: If Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle DEF (in that exact vertex correspondence), which angle in Triangle DEF is equal to angle A?
distractors: None of the angles are guaranteed equal

cong_l2_new2.technicalIntricacy: The order of the letters in a congruence statement (ABC ≅ DEF) directly specifies the correspondence: A matches D, B matches E, and C matches F, so their respective angles and sides are guaranteed equal in that exact pairing.
cong_l2_new2.realPurpose: Reading congruence statements correctly (matching vertices in the stated order) is essential for correctly identifying which specific sides and angles are equal.

variants.question: A student claims two triangles are congruent because two of their sides and one angle are equal, without checking whether the equal angle is the angle INCLUDED between the two equal sides. Why is this reasoning risky, and what does the SAS criterion actually require?
variants.answer: SAS specifically requires the equal angle to be the INCLUDED angle (the angle formed directly between the two equal sides); if the equal angle lies elsewhere, the two sides and one angle alone do not guarantee the triangles are congruent
distractors: The student's reasoning is valid — any two equal sides and any one equal angle are always enough to prove two triangles congruent
The triangles can only be congruent if all three sides are also equal, making the angle irrelevant
The triangles are automatically congruent as long as the two equal sides are the two longest sides in each triangle

ge_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: When the equal angle is not the included angle (sometimes called the 'SSA case'), it is possible to construct two genuinely different, non-congruent triangles that still share those two side lengths and that one angle, so congruence cannot be concluded without confirming the angle's exact position.
ge_l3_t2.realPurpose: Understanding exactly which combinations of equal parts guarantee congruence (and which don't) prevents incorrect geometric proofs and is essential for rigorous mathematical reasoning.

variants.question: A student claims two triangles are congruent because all three corresponding angles are equal (AAA). What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Equal corresponding angles (AAA) only proves the triangles are SIMILAR (same shape), not necessarily congruent (same shape AND size); the triangles could be different sizes while still having identical angles, so AAA alone is not a valid congruence criterion
distractors: The student is correct — AAA is a fully valid congruence criterion, just like SSS or SAS
AAA only fails to prove congruence if the triangles are right-angled
Triangles with equal angles must always also have equal side lengths

cong_l3_new.technicalIntricacy: Similar triangles have identical angles but can be scaled versions of each other with completely different side lengths; congruence additionally requires matching SIZE, which is why a valid congruence criterion must always involve at least one equal side length.
cong_l3_new.realPurpose: This distinction between similarity (same shape) and congruence (same shape AND size) is fundamental to geometry, and confusing the two leads to invalid proofs.

variants.question: How many flat faces does a cube have?
How many edges does a cube have?
How many vertices (corners) does a cube have?
Which three-dimensional shape has exactly one flat circular face, one curved surface, and one vertex (a point)?

ge_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: Three-dimensional shapes are described by counting their faces (flat or curved surfaces), edges (where two faces meet), and vertices (where edges meet at a point), which together define the shape's structure.
ge_l1_t6.realPurpose: Understanding the properties of 3D shapes is essential for fields like architecture, packaging design, and manufacturing, where the number of faces or edges directly affects how a shape can be built or folded from a flat pattern.

variants.question: A polyhedron has {{faces}} faces and {{vertices}} vertices. Using Euler's formula (Faces + Vertices − Edges = 2), how many edges does it have?

3d_l2_new1.technicalIntricacy: Euler's formula (Faces + Vertices − Edges = 2) holds true for every simple polyhedron, so rearranging it to Edges = Faces + Vertices − 2 lets you calculate the number of edges directly from the other two counts.
3d_l2_new1.realPurpose: Euler's formula is a powerful shortcut for checking or completing the face/edge/vertex counts of any polyhedron without having to physically count every edge.

variants.question: A polyhedron has {{faces}} faces and {{edges}} edges. Using Euler's formula (Faces + Vertices − Edges = 2), how many vertices does it have?

3d_l2_new2.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging Euler's formula to solve for vertices gives Vertices = Edges − Faces + 2, letting you calculate the missing vertex count whenever the faces and edges are already known.
3d_l2_new2.realPurpose: Being able to solve Euler's formula for any one of its three variables makes it a flexible tool for checking the consistency of a described polyhedron.

variants.question: A student believes any 6 identical squares arranged in ANY layout can be folded into a cube. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Not every arrangement of six squares folds into a closed cube — only specific arrangements (valid 'nets' of a cube, of which there are exactly 11) fold correctly without overlapping faces or leaving gaps; an arbitrary arrangement of six squares will often fail to fold into a proper cube
distractors: The student is correct — any arrangement of six identical squares always folds into a valid cube
A cube can only be formed from exactly 4 squares arranged in a single row
Only arrangements with all six squares in a single straight row can fold into a cube

3d_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: A 'net' is a specific 2D arrangement of faces that folds into a 3D solid without gaps or overlaps; a cube has exactly 11 distinct valid nets out of the many more ways six squares could theoretically be arranged.
3d_l3_new1.realPurpose: Understanding valid nets is essential for packaging design, where a flat sheet of material must fold into a precise 3D box shape with no wasted material or gaps.

variants.question: A student calculates a shape's edges using Faces + Vertices − Edges = 2 but forgets to rearrange the formula, writing Edges = Faces + Vertices, without subtracting 2. What effect does this mistake have?
variants.answer: Forgetting to subtract 2 after rearranging Euler's formula (Edges = Faces + Vertices − 2) makes the calculated number of edges exactly 2 too many for every single polyhedron, since the formula only balances correctly when that constant 2 is included
distractors: The mistake has no effect, since the constant 2 is optional in Euler's formula
This mistake only matters for shapes with curved surfaces, not polyhedra
The correct fix is to subtract 2 from the faces instead of from the final edge count

3d_l3_new2.technicalIntricacy: Euler's formula is a fixed equation (F + V − E = 2); correctly rearranging it to solve for any one variable requires carefully moving every term, including the constant 2, to the correct side of the equation.
3d_l3_new2.realPurpose: This is a common algebraic rearrangement mistake, and checking the final formula against a known simple polyhedron (like a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2) is a reliable way to catch it.

variants.question: A shape that can be folded along a line so that both halves match exactly has what kind of symmetry?
A shape that looks exactly the same after being turned part-way around a central point has what kind of symmetry?
The line along which a shape is folded to produce two matching halves is called the:

ge_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: Line symmetry is about reflecting a shape across a line so both halves match, while rotational symmetry is about rotating a shape around a fixed centre point so it looks unchanged at certain angles — two related but distinct types of symmetry.
ge_l1_t5.realPurpose: Recognising these symmetry types explains the design of everything from snowflakes and flags to logos and architecture, where symmetry is often used deliberately for visual balance.

ge_l2_t4.questionTemplate: A line of symmetry divides an isosceles triangle's apex angle of {{totalAngle}}° into two exactly equal halves. What is the measure of each half?
ge_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: A line of symmetry splits a symmetric figure into two identical mirror-image halves, so any angle it passes through is divided into two exactly equal parts.
ge_l2_t4.realPurpose: Understanding symmetry and equal angle division is used constantly in geometric constructions, such as bisecting angles with a compass and straightedge.

variants.question: A regular polygon has {{sides}} sides. What is its order of rotational symmetry (i.e., how many times it looks unchanged during one full 360° rotation)?

sym_l2_new.technicalIntricacy: A regular polygon's order of rotational symmetry always equals its number of sides, since rotating it by (360° ÷ number of sides) always maps the shape exactly onto itself.
sym_l2_new.realPurpose: This direct relationship between sides and rotational symmetry order explains why regular polygons are used so often in flags, logos and decorative patterns.

variants.question: A student says a shape with rotational symmetry must also always have line symmetry. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: Rotational symmetry and line symmetry are independent properties — a shape can have one without the other; for example, a pinwheel-like shape has rotational symmetry (looks the same after a partial turn) but no line of symmetry at all
distractors: The student is correct — any shape with rotational symmetry automatically also has line symmetry
Line symmetry always implies rotational symmetry, but not the other way around
No shape can ever have both rotational and line symmetry at the same time

sym_l3_new1.technicalIntricacy: Line symmetry and rotational symmetry test for two different kinds of self-matching (reflecting across a line vs. rotating around a point), and a shape can possess either, both, or neither, independently of the other.
sym_l3_new1.realPurpose: Recognising that these are independent properties prevents an easy but incorrect assumption when analysing the symmetry of an unfamiliar shape.

variants.question: A student assumes a rectangle (that is not a square) has 4 lines of symmetry, just like a square does. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: A non-square rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of each pair of opposite sides), not 4; a square has extra symmetry (4 lines total, including both diagonals) specifically because all four of its sides are equal, which a general rectangle's sides are not
distractors: The student is correct — all rectangles, square or not, have exactly 4 lines of symmetry
A non-square rectangle has zero lines of symmetry
A non-square rectangle has exactly 1 line of symmetry, running through one diagonal

sym_l3_new2.technicalIntricacy: A square's extra pair of diagonal symmetry lines only works because all four sides are equal; in a non-square rectangle, folding along a diagonal does NOT produce two matching halves, so only the two midline folds remain valid lines of symmetry.
sym_l3_new2.realPurpose: This distinction highlights how a shape's extra properties (like equal sides in a square) can unlock extra symmetry beyond what a more general shape in the same family possesses.

variants.question: Which formula correctly gives the area of a triangle?
Which formula correctly gives the circumference of a circle?
Which formula correctly gives the area of a circle?

mn_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Each mensuration formula reflects the geometric structure of its shape — a triangle's area is half of the parallelogram it could form with an identical triangle, while a circle's measurements depend on the fixed ratio π between circumference and diameter.
mn_l1_t1.realPurpose: Correctly recalling these formulas is essential before any real-world area or length calculation, from flooring a room to fencing a circular garden.

variants.question: Perimeter is always measured in single (linear) units, like cm or m, because it represents:
variants.answer: The total length of the boundary around a shape
distractors: The amount of two-dimensional surface covered by a shape
The amount of three-dimensional space enclosed by a shape
The number of sides a shape has

variants.question: Area is always measured in square units, like cm<sup>2</sup> or m<sup>2</sup>, because it represents:
variants.answer: The amount of two-dimensional surface covered by a shape
distractors: The total length of the boundary around a shape
The amount of three-dimensional space enclosed by a shape
The average of the shape's length and breadth

mn_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: The unit type attached to a measurement (linear, square, or cubic) is not arbitrary — it directly reflects whether the quantity being measured is one-dimensional (length), two-dimensional (surface), or three-dimensional (volume).
mn_l1_t2.realPurpose: Using the correct unit type prevents serious real-world errors, such as confusing how much fencing (perimeter) a garden needs with how much turf (area) it needs.

variants.question: Which formula correctly gives the volume of a cube?
Which formula correctly gives the volume of a cuboid (rectangular box)?
Which formula correctly gives the volume of a cylinder?

mn_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Every volume formula reflects a solid's specific shape — a cube's identical sides cube neatly together, a cuboid multiplies its three distinct dimensions, and a cylinder combines a circle's area with its height.
mn_l1_t3.realPurpose: Correct volume formulas are essential for real tasks like calculating how much liquid a container can hold or how much material is needed to fill a mould.

variants.question: What term describes the total area of all the outer faces of a 3D solid?
How many faces does a cube have?
How many faces does a cuboid (rectangular box) have?

mn_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Surface area measures the total two-dimensional 'skin' covering a three-dimensional solid, found by adding up the areas of every individual face; cubes and cuboids both have exactly six rectangular (or square) faces.
mn_l1_t4.realPurpose: Surface area calculations are used to determine how much material, like wrapping paper or paint, is needed to cover the entire outside of a solid object.

mn_l2_t1.questionTemplate: What is the circumference of a circle with radius {{radius}} cm? (Use π = 22/7 and Circumference = 2 × π × radius)
mn_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: Circumference scales directly (linearly) with radius, since it is simply the constant 2π multiplied by the radius; doubling the radius exactly doubles the circumference.
mn_l2_t1.realPurpose: Circumference calculations are used to determine the length of material needed to go around circular objects, such as fencing a circular plot or fitting a belt around a wheel.

mn_l2_t2.questionTemplate: What is the area of a triangle with a base of {{base}} cm and a height of {{height}} cm? (Area = ½ × base × height)
mn_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: A triangle's area is exactly half of the rectangle (or parallelogram) that shares its base and height, which is why the formula includes the factor of ½.
mn_l2_t2.realPurpose: Triangle area calculations are used in construction, land surveying, and anywhere triangular sections of material or land must be measured.

variants.question: A circle has a diameter of {{diameter}} cm. A student calculates its area using the formula π × radius<sup>2</sup>, but plugs in the diameter ({{diameter}}) directly instead of first finding the radius. What is the mistake, and what is the correct area? (Use π = 22/7)
variants.answer: {{correctArea}} cm<sup>2</sup>, found by first halving the diameter to get the radius ({{radius}} cm) before squaring it
distractors: {{wrongArea}} cm<sup>2</sup> is correct, found by using the diameter directly in the formula πr<sup>2</sup>
{{correctArea}} cm<sup>2</sup> is correct, but only because the diameter happens to equal the radius in this case
The area cannot be found unless the circumference is also known

mn_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Since diameter = 2 × radius, using the diameter directly in place of the radius squares a value twice as large, making the calculated area four times too big (because (2r)<sup>2</sup> = 4r<sup>2</sup>) — the diameter must always be halved to get the radius before applying the area formula.
mn_l3_t1.realPurpose: This is one of the most common mensuration mistakes, and avoiding it is essential whenever a problem gives the diameter instead of directly stating the radius.

variants.question: A rectangular garden has a length of {{length}} m and a breadth of {{breadth}} m. A student calculates its perimeter by adding the length and breadth just once, getting {{wrongPerimeter}} m. What is the mistake, and what is the correct perimeter?
variants.answer: {{correctPerimeter}} m, found using Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth), since a rectangle has two lengths and two breadths
distractors: {{wrongPerimeter}} m is correct, found by simply adding the length and breadth once
{{areaProduct}} m, found by multiplying the length and breadth together
The perimeter cannot be found without also knowing the rectangle's area

mn_l3_t2.technicalIntricacy: A rectangle's boundary consists of two lengths and two breadths, not just one of each, so the perimeter formula must count each side twice: Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth), not simply length + breadth.
mn_l3_t2.realPurpose: Getting perimeter right matters directly in real tasks like buying enough fencing for a garden or trim for a room, where underestimating by half would leave the job incomplete.

mn_l2_t3.questionTemplate: What is the volume of a cuboid with length {{length}} cm, breadth {{breadth}} cm, and height {{height}} cm? (Volume = length × breadth × height)
mn_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: A cuboid's volume is found by multiplying all three of its dimensions together, since volume measures the three-dimensional space enclosed by combining length, width and height.
mn_l2_t3.realPurpose: This calculation is used to determine the capacity of boxes, rooms, containers, and any rectangular three-dimensional space.

mn_l2_t4.questionTemplate: What is the volume of a cube with a side length of {{side}} cm? (Volume = side³)
mn_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: A cube has all three dimensions equal, so its volume formula simplifies to the side length raised to the power of three (cubed), rather than needing three separate measurements multiplied together.
mn_l2_t4.realPurpose: Cube volume calculations are used for storage boxes, dice, sugar cubes, and any object with equal length, width and height.

variants.question: A student calculates the volume of a cuboid with length {{length}} cm, breadth {{breadth}} cm and height {{height}} cm by adding the three dimensions together, getting {{wrongSum}} cm³. What is the mistake, and what is the correct volume?
variants.answer: {{correctVolume}} cm³, found by MULTIPLYING length × breadth × height (not adding them)
distractors: {{wrongSum}} cm³ is correct, found by adding the three dimensions together
{{correctVolume}} cm³, but only because the numbers happened to work out the same either way
The volume cannot be found without knowing the cuboid's surface area first

mn_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: Volume represents the three-dimensional space enclosed by a solid, which requires combining all three dimensions multiplicatively (length × breadth × height); adding them together produces a one-dimensional length total that has no meaningful connection to enclosed volume.
mn_l3_t3.realPurpose: This distinction between adding and multiplying dimensions is essential whenever calculating volume, since confusing the two produces answers that are wrong by a large and unpredictable margin.

variants.question: A cube has a side length of {{side}} cm and a volume of {{originalVolume}} cm³. A student doubles the side length to {{newSide}} cm and assumes the volume will also simply double. What is the mistake, and what does the volume actually become?
variants.answer: The volume becomes {{correctNewVolume}} cm³ (8 times larger than the original {{originalVolume}} cm³), since doubling every dimension of a cube multiplies its volume by 2³ = 8, not just 2
distractors: The volume simply doubles to {{doubledVolume}} cm³, matching the doubled side length
The volume stays exactly the same at {{originalVolume}} cm³, since only the side length changed
The volume increases by exactly 2 cm³, regardless of the original size

mn_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Because a cube's volume depends on three dimensions multiplied together (side × side × side), doubling the side length doubles the volume three separate times (2 × 2 × 2 = 8), not just once, which is why volume grows so much faster than linear side length.
mn_l3_t4.realPurpose: This cubic growth relationship explains why even a small increase in the size of a container or object can lead to a dramatically larger volume or capacity.

variants.question: Which measure of central tendency is found by adding all the values together and dividing by the total number of values?
Which measure of central tendency is the middle value when the data is arranged in order?
Which measure of central tendency is the value that occurs most frequently in a data set?
Which measure represents the difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set?

dh_l1_t1.technicalIntricacy: Mean, median, mode and range each summarise a data set differently: mean captures the overall balance point, median captures the middle position, mode captures the most common value, and range captures the spread — no single one tells the whole story alone.
dh_l1_t1.realPurpose: Choosing the right measure of central tendency matters — for example, median is often more informative than mean for data with extreme outliers, like income or house prices.

variants.question: Which type of graph uses bars of different heights to compare categories of data?
Which type of graph uses a circle divided into slices to show how a total is divided into parts?
Which type of graph uses points connected by lines to show how data changes over time?

dh_l1_t3.technicalIntricacy: Different graph types are suited to different kinds of data stories — bar graphs for comparing separate categories, pie charts for showing proportions of a whole, and line graphs for tracking continuous change over time.
dh_l1_t3.realPurpose: Choosing the right graph type makes data far easier to understand at a glance, which is why news reports and scientific papers carefully choose which graph style fits their data best.

variants.question: What term describes a range of values grouped together in a frequency distribution table, such as '10–20'?
What is the term for a small mark used to record occurrences while counting data, often grouped in sets of five?

dh_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Organising raw data into class intervals and recording occurrences with tally marks are both practical techniques for turning a large, disorganised set of individual values into a clear, manageable frequency table.
dh_l1_t4.realPurpose: These organisational tools are the essential first step before creating any graph or calculating any statistic from a large, real-world data set.

variants.question: Find the mean of the following data set: {{v1}}, {{v2}}, {{v3}}, {{v4}}, {{v5}}.

dh_l2_t1.technicalIntricacy: The mean is calculated by summing every value in the data set and dividing by how many values there are, giving a single number that represents the data set's overall balance point.
dh_l2_t1.realPurpose: The mean is the most commonly used average in everyday life, from calculating a class's average test score to a team's average points per game.

variants.question: A bag contains {{total}} balls, of which {{favourable}} are red. If one ball is drawn at random, what is the probability that it is red?

dh_l2_t2.technicalIntricacy: Probability is expressed as a fraction: the number of favourable outcomes (red balls) over the total number of equally likely possible outcomes (all balls in the bag), assuming each ball is equally likely to be drawn.
dh_l2_t2.realPurpose: This fraction-based approach to probability is used to calculate the odds in games, quality control sampling, and genetic inheritance predictions.

variants.question: Find the median of the following data set (arrange the values in order first): {{v1}}, {{v2}}, {{v3}}, {{v4}}, {{v5}}.

dh_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Finding the median requires first sorting the data into ascending (or descending) order, then identifying the single middle value when there is an odd number of data points.
dh_l2_t3.realPurpose: The median is especially useful for summarising data that includes outliers, since it isn't distorted by extremely high or low values the way the mean can be.

variants.question: Find the mode of the following data set: {{modeValue}}, {{other1}}, {{modeValue}}, {{other2}}, {{other3}}.

dh_l2_t4.technicalIntricacy: The mode is simply the value that appears most often in a data set, found by counting how many times each distinct value occurs and identifying the one with the highest count.
dh_l2_t4.realPurpose: The mode is especially useful for categorical data (like favourite colours or shoe sizes), where calculating a mean or median wouldn't make practical sense.

variants.question: A small company has several employees earning around ₹{{typicalSalary}} per year, but the owner earns ₹{{ownerSalary}} per year. A student calculates the mean of all salaries (including the owner's) and concludes this mean represents a "typical" employee's salary. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
variants.answer: The mean is heavily skewed upward by the one extreme outlier (the owner's very high salary), so it does not represent what a typical employee actually earns; the median would give a far more realistic 'typical' value, since it is not affected by extreme outliers
distractors: The student's conclusion is correct — the mean always represents a typical value in any data set, regardless of outliers
The mean is invalid here only because there are too few employees at the company, not because of the outlier
The mode should have been used instead of the mean, since mode is always more accurate for salary data

dh_l3_t1.technicalIntricacy: Because the mean is calculated by summing every value and dividing by the count, a single extremely large (or small) value can pull the mean far away from where most of the data actually lies; the median, which depends only on the middle position of ordered data, is much more resistant to such outliers.
dh_l3_t1.realPurpose: This is why statistics like median household income are often reported instead of mean income, to avoid a small number of very high earners distorting the picture of what a 'typical' person earns.

variants.question: A student computes the median by finding the value at the middle POSITION of a list, without first sorting the values in order. What is the mistake in this reasoning?
variants.answer: The median can only be found correctly after the data has been sorted in order (ascending or descending); simply picking the value that happens to sit in the middle position of an unsorted list can give a completely wrong answer, since the median is defined specifically as the middle VALUE once the data is properly ordered
distractors: The student is correct — the median is always whichever value happens to be listed in the middle position, sorted or not
Sorting the data is only necessary for calculating the mean, not the median
The median can only be calculated correctly if the data set has an even number of values

dh_l3_t3.technicalIntricacy: The median is defined as the middle value once a data set is arranged in increasing or decreasing order; picking whichever value happens to occupy the middle position of an unsorted list is essentially arbitrary and has no reliable connection to the actual middle value of the data.
dh_l3_t3.realPurpose: This is a critical first step that's easy to forget, and skipping it is one of the most common errors students make when first learning to calculate the median.

variants.question: A student assumes a data set can only have one mode, and gets confused when a data set has two values tied for the most frequent. What is the more accurate understanding here?
variants.answer: A data set CAN have more than one mode (called 'bimodal' if there are exactly two, or 'multimodal' if there are more); it's also possible for a data set to have no mode at all if every value appears the same number of times — mode isn't guaranteed to be a single unique value the way mean or median typically are
distractors: The student is correct — every data set must have exactly one single mode, with no exceptions
A data set with two equally frequent values simply has no mode at all, and neither value can be used
In cases of a tie, the mode is always found by averaging the two most frequent values together

dh_l3_t4.technicalIntricacy: Unlike the mean (a single calculated average) or the median (a single middle position), the mode is defined purely by frequency count, so a data set can legitimately have zero, one, two ('bimodal'), or more ('multimodal') values that are all tied for the highest frequency.
dh_l3_t4.realPurpose: Recognising that data can be bimodal or multimodal is important for accurately describing real data sets, such as exam scores that cluster around two very different common results.

variants.question: What is the probability of an event that is impossible?
What is the probability of an event that is absolutely certain to happen?
The probability of an event is calculated as the number of favourable outcomes divided by:
variants.answer: The total number of possible outcomes
distractors: The number of trials already conducted

dh_l1_t2.technicalIntricacy: Probability is defined on a fixed scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), calculated as the ratio of favourable outcomes to all equally likely possible outcomes, which is why it can never be negative or greater than 1.
dh_l1_t2.realPurpose: This precise definition of probability underlies risk assessment in insurance, weather forecasting, quality control, and any situation involving uncertain outcomes.

variants.question: A student flips a fair coin and gets heads {{streak}} times in a row. The student concludes the next flip is "due" to be tails, since heads has come up so many times already. What is the mistake, and what is the actual probability of getting tails on the next flip?
variants.answer: Each coin flip is an independent event, so previous results have no influence on the next flip; the probability of tails on the next flip remains exactly 1/2 (50%), regardless of the streak of heads
distractors: The student is correct — after several heads in a row, tails genuinely becomes more likely on the next flip
The probability of tails on the next flip drops to 0, since the coin has already 'used up' its chance for tails
The coin must be biased if heads comes up several times in a row, so the true probability cannot be calculated

prob_l3_new.technicalIntricacy: This reasoning error is known as the gambler's fallacy: because each coin flip is a completely independent event with no memory of past outcomes, the coin does not 'owe' a tails result, and the probability of tails remains fixed at 1/2 on every single flip, no matter how long the current streak is.
prob_l3_new.realPurpose: Understanding independence between events is critical for correctly reasoning about games of chance, insurance risk, and avoiding costly misconceptions in gambling and everyday probability judgments.

variants.question: In Simple Interest, is interest calculated only on the original principal, or on the principal plus any previously earned interest?
Which typically grows an investment faster over multiple years: Simple Interest or Compound Interest?

distractorPool: A randomly chosen amount, unrelated to the principal
Both Simple Interest and Compound Interest always produce exactly the same result over any number of years
ar_l1_t4.technicalIntricacy: Simple Interest is calculated only on the original principal every year, growing by the same fixed amount annually, while Compound Interest is recalculated each year on the growing total (principal plus previously earned interest), causing it to grow faster over time.
ar_l1_t4.realPurpose: Understanding the difference between simple and compound interest is essential for comparing real financial products like loans and savings accounts, where compounding can make a significant difference over many years.

ge_l2_t3.questionTemplate: A polygon has {{sides}} sides. Using the formula (Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°, where n is the number of sides), what is the sum of its interior angles?
ge_l2_t3.technicalIntricacy: Any polygon can be divided into (n − 2) triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex, and since every triangle's angles sum to 180°, multiplying by the number of triangles gives the polygon's total interior angle sum.
ge_l2_t3.realPurpose: This formula lets you calculate the interior angle sum of any polygon, from a triangle up to complex many-sided shapes, using just the number of sides.

variants.question: If every element of Set A is also an element of Set B, then A is called a:
A subset that does not equal the original set (that is, B contains at least one extra element not in A) is called a:
The set containing every possible subset of a set A, including the empty set and A itself, is called the:

se_l1_t5.technicalIntricacy: A subset requires every element of the smaller set to appear in the larger set; a proper subset adds the extra condition that the larger set must contain at least one more element; the power set collects every one of these possible subsets together into one new set.
se_l1_t5.realPurpose: These subset relationships describe how one collection can be fully contained within another, which is the basis for hierarchies and category structures used throughout mathematics and computing.

variants.question: The set of all elements that are in Set A but NOT in Set B is called:
variants.answer: The difference of A and B (A − B)

variants.question: Within a universal set, the set of all elements NOT in A is called:
Two sets that share no elements in common are called:

distractorPool: The difference of A and B (A − B)
The union of A and B
se_l1_t6.technicalIntricacy: The difference A − B keeps only A's elements that are missing from B, the complement A′ flips this idea to look at everything outside A within the universal set, and disjoint sets are simply the special case where A and B share no elements at all.
se_l1_t6.realPurpose: These operations let you describe exactly what belongs to one group and not another, which is exactly how database queries and search filters exclude or isolate specific records.

variants.question: What does the notation n(A) represent?
variants.answer: The number of elements in set A

variants.question: What does 'x ∈ A' mean?
variants.answer: x is an element of set A

variants.question: What does 'x ∉ A' mean?
variants.answer: x is NOT an element of set A

distractorPool: The number of elements in set A
x is an element of set A
x is NOT an element of set A
The sum of every element in A
se_l1_t7.technicalIntricacy: n(A) counts elements while ∈ and ∉ describe membership of a single item; all three are compact symbols that replace a full sentence with a single precise piece of notation.
se_l1_t7.realPurpose: Fluency with this notation is essential for reading set theory (and later, algebra and functions) without constantly translating symbols back into plain English.

variants.question: In a Venn diagram of two overlapping sets A and B, what does the region where the circles overlap represent?
In a Venn diagram of two overlapping sets A and B, what does the entire region covered by both circles together represent?
In a Venn diagram, what does the surrounding rectangle represent?

se_l1_t8.technicalIntricacy: A Venn diagram gives every set operation a visual region: the overlap is the intersection, both circles together form the union, and the rectangle enclosing everything represents the universal set being considered.
se_l1_t8.realPurpose: Being able to read regions off a Venn diagram directly is often faster and clearer than working with symbolic set notation alone, especially when checking a result makes sense.

variants.question: A set has 3 elements. How many PROPER subsets does it have (that is, subsets excluding the full set itself)?
A set has 4 elements. How many PROPER subsets does it have (that is, subsets excluding the full set itself)?

se_l1_t9.technicalIntricacy: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets in total; excluding only the set itself (which is the one subset that isn't 'proper') leaves 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets.
se_l1_t9.realPurpose: Distinguishing 'all subsets' from 'proper subsets' matters whenever a problem specifically excludes the full original set from being counted as one of its own subsets.

variants.question: Which is the correct roster form of the set of all even numbers between 1 and 9?
Which is the correct roster form of the set of the first four multiples of 3?
Which is the correct roster form of the set of all factors of 10?

se_l1_t10.technicalIntricacy: Building a roster form means translating a described property (evenness, being a multiple, being a factor) into an actual, explicit list of the numbers that satisfy it.
se_l1_t10.realPurpose: This translation skill is what makes set-builder descriptions useful in the first place — the description only has value if it can be reliably converted into a concrete listed set.

se_l2_t5.questionTemplate: Set A has {{countA}} elements and Set B has {{countB}} elements. If n(A ∪ B) = {{unionVal}}, how many elements are common to both sets (n(A ∩ B))?
se_l2_t5.technicalIntricacy: Rearranging n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) to solve for the overlap gives n(A ∩ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∪ B), the same subtraction pattern used to find the union, just applied in reverse.
se_l2_t5.realPurpose: Working backwards from a known union size to find the overlap is exactly how real overlapping-group problems are often presented, such as finding how many students take both of two subjects when only the totals are given.

variants.question: Multiplying two integers with the SAME sign (both positive or both negative) gives a result that is:
Multiplying two integers with DIFFERENT signs (one positive, one negative) gives a result that is:
Dividing a negative integer by a negative integer gives a result that is:

int_l1_new2.technicalIntricacy: Multiplication and division share the same sign rule: matching signs (both positive or both negative) always produce a positive result, while mismatched signs always produce a negative result.
int_l1_new2.realPurpose: This single consistent rule covers every possible sign combination for both multiplying and dividing integers, making it one of the most frequently applied facts in algebra.

variants.question: On a number line, integers increase in value as you move in which direction?
Which of these integers lies furthest to the LEFT on a number line: −10, −2, 0, 5?
Which integer is the immediate successor (one more than) of −6?
Which integer is the immediate predecessor (one less than) of −6?

int_l1_new3.technicalIntricacy: A number line orders every integer left to right from smallest to largest, so the leftmost of any group is always the smallest, and moving one step right or left gives the successor or predecessor.
int_l1_new3.realPurpose: Picturing integers on a number line makes comparing and ordering negative and positive values far more intuitive than working with the symbols alone.

variants.question: Is zero a positive integer, a negative integer, or neither?
What is the sum of any integer and its additive inverse?
What is the additive inverse of −12?

int_l1_new4.technicalIntricacy: Zero sits exactly at the boundary between positive and negative integers, belonging to neither group, and it is precisely this 'boundary' role that makes it the result whenever an integer is added to its own additive inverse.
int_l1_new4.realPurpose: Recognising zero's special status and the additive inverse property underpins solving simple equations, where adding the inverse of a term is used to cancel it out.

variants.question: What is the absolute value of 0?
Can the absolute value of an integer ever be negative?
variants.answer: No — absolute value is always zero or positive
distractors: Yes, whenever the integer itself is negative

variants.question: Which has the greater absolute value: −15 or 9?

int_l1_new5.technicalIntricacy: Absolute value measures distance from zero, and distance can never be negative, so |0| = 0 exactly, and comparing absolute values means comparing distances from zero rather than the signed values themselves.
int_l1_new5.realPurpose: This distinction between an integer's value and its distance from zero is essential whenever only the 'size' of a change matters, regardless of its direction.

variants.question: Which list correctly orders these integers from smallest to largest: −7, 3, −2, 0?
Is −1 greater than or less than 0?

int_l1_new6.technicalIntricacy: Ordering a mixed list of integers means placing every negative value before zero, and zero before every positive value, with more negative numbers coming before less negative ones.
int_l1_new6.realPurpose: Correctly ordering integers is essential for reading temperature scales, elevation charts, and account balances where negative values are common.

variants.question: What is the effect of multiplying any integer by −1?
variants.answer: It flips the sign, giving the integer's additive inverse
distractors: It always makes the result negative
It has no effect on the number

variants.question: What is −(−8) equal to?

int_l1_new7.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying by −1 reverses an integer's sign without changing its size, so applying it twice (as in −(−8)) returns the original positive value.
int_l1_new7.realPurpose: This 'double negative cancels out' behaviour appears throughout algebra whenever a negative sign is applied to an already-negative expression.

variants.question: Is −9 an integer?
distractors: Only if written as a fraction

variants.question: Is 4.5 an integer?
variants.answer: No — integers must be whole numbers, with no fractional or decimal part

variants.question: Is 0 an integer?
distractors: Only as a whole number, never as an integer

int_l1_new8.technicalIntricacy: Integers include zero and all positive and negative whole numbers, but never values with a fractional or decimal remainder, which is exactly why 4.5 fails to qualify while −9 and 0 both do.
int_l1_new8.realPurpose: Being able to quickly identify whether a value is an integer is the first step before applying any integer-specific rule, such as the sign rules for multiplication.

variants.question: Subtracting an integer b from a (that is, a − b) is mathematically the same as:
variants.answer: Adding the additive inverse of b to a (a + (−b))

variants.question: If you subtract a positive integer from another integer, does the result increase or decrease?

int_l1_new9.technicalIntricacy: Subtraction is formally defined in terms of addition — a − b always equals a + (−b) — which is why subtracting a positive value always decreases the result, moving further left on the number line.
int_l1_new9.realPurpose: Framing subtraction as 'adding the opposite' is the single idea that makes subtracting negative integers (where the result increases instead) consistent and predictable rather than a separate special case.

int_l2_new3.technicalIntricacy: The sign of the product depends only on whether the two integers share the same sign (positive result) or opposite signs (negative result), regardless of how large either number is.
int_l2_new3.realPurpose: Integer multiplication models repeated combined changes, such as calculating the total change after several equal temperature drops or repeated equal withdrawals.

int_l2_new4.technicalIntricacy: Dividing integers follows the same sign rule as multiplication: a negative dividend with a positive divisor gives a negative quotient, matching what happens when the multiplication is reversed.
int_l2_new4.realPurpose: Integer division is used whenever a total change (like a total temperature drop) must be split evenly across a number of equal steps.

int_l2_new5.technicalIntricacy: Each absolute value must be found first (stripping away any sign), and only then are the two resulting non-negative numbers subtracted — skipping the absolute value step and subtracting the signed integers directly gives a completely different result.
int_l2_new5.realPurpose: This combination of operations tests whether absolute value is applied before, rather than after, another operation, a common source of order-of-operations mistakes.

variants.question: A student claims −10 is greater than −3, reasoning that '10 is bigger than 3, so −10 must be bigger too.' What is the mistake?
variants.answer: For negative numbers, a larger magnitude actually means a SMALLER value, since a bigger negative number sits further to the left on the number line; −10 is actually less than −3 (−10 < −3), not greater
distractors: The student is correct — a bigger magnitude always means a bigger value, regardless of sign
−10 and −3 are equal in value, since both numbers are negative
Negative numbers cannot be compared to one another at all

int_l3_new3.technicalIntricacy: Comparing negative integers works in the opposite direction to comparing their magnitudes: as the magnitude of a negative number grows, its actual value shrinks, since it moves further from zero in the negative direction.
int_l3_new3.realPurpose: This reversal is one of the most common integer-ordering mistakes, and avoiding it is essential for correctly reading scales like temperature or elevation where negative values are routine.

variants.question: Fractions that have the same denominator are called:
Fractions that have different denominators are called:
To add or subtract unlike fractions, what must be found first?

frac_l1_new3.technicalIntricacy: Like fractions already share equal-sized parts (the same denominator) and so can be combined directly, while unlike fractions must first be rewritten over a shared denominator before their numerators mean the same thing.
frac_l1_new3.realPurpose: Recognising whether fractions are like or unlike is the very first step in any fraction addition or subtraction problem, determining whether extra conversion work is needed.

variants.question: A fraction is in its simplest form (lowest terms) when:
variants.answer: The numerator and denominator share no common factor other than 1
distractors: The numerator is smaller than the denominator
The denominator is a multiple of 10
The fraction has an odd denominator

variants.question: What is 12/18 written in its simplest form?
What is 15/25 written in its simplest form?

frac_l1_new4.technicalIntricacy: A fraction reaches its simplest form only once the numerator and denominator have been divided by their greatest common factor, leaving no shared factor larger than 1 behind.
frac_l1_new4.realPurpose: Simplified fractions are easier to interpret, compare, and combine, and are almost always the expected final form for an answer.

variants.question: A fraction with a numerator of 1, such as 1/4, is called a:
What is the reciprocal of 3/7?
What is the reciprocal of the whole number 5?

frac_l1_new5.technicalIntricacy: A unit fraction always has a numerator of exactly 1, while a reciprocal is formed by flipping any fraction upside down (including a whole number, which is really a fraction over 1).
frac_l1_new5.realPurpose: Reciprocals are essential for fraction division, since dividing by a fraction is defined as multiplying by its reciprocal.

variants.question: Which is greater: 3/8 or 5/8?
Which is greater: 2/9 or 7/9?
When two fractions share the same denominator, the one with the larger numerator is:

frac_l1_new6.technicalIntricacy: When fractions are already split into equal-sized parts (a shared denominator), simply comparing how many of those parts each fraction has (the numerator) tells you immediately which fraction is larger.
frac_l1_new6.realPurpose: This is the simplest fraction comparison case, and it is the foundation for the more general method used once denominators differ.

variants.question: Which is greater: 3/4 or 5/8?
Which is greater: 2/3 or 3/5?
To compare two fractions with different denominators, one reliable method is to:
variants.answer: Convert both to a common denominator (or cross-multiply) before comparing
distractors: Assume the fraction with the bigger denominator is always bigger

frac_l1_new7.technicalIntricacy: Fractions with different denominators represent parts of different sizes, so they cannot be compared directly by their numerators alone until they are rewritten over a shared denominator (or compared using cross-multiplication).
frac_l1_new7.realPurpose: This comparison method is essential whenever two differently-split quantities, such as different-sized recipe portions, need to be judged fairly against each other.

variants.question: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
Which fraction is equivalent to 2/5?
Two fractions are equivalent when:
variants.answer: They represent the same value, even though their numerators and denominators differ
distractors: They have exactly the same numerator
They have exactly the same denominator
They always simplify to different values

frac_l1_new8.technicalIntricacy: Equivalent fractions all represent the same point on the number line, produced by multiplying (or dividing) both the numerator and denominator of one fraction by the same non-zero number.
frac_l1_new8.realPurpose: Recognising equivalent fractions is essential before adding, subtracting, or comparing fractions, since converting to a matching equivalent form is how a common denominator is created.

variants.question: A number written as a whole number together with a proper fraction, such as 2¾, is called a:
In the mixed number 2¾, what is the whole-number part?
In the mixed number 2¾, what is the fractional part?

frac_l1_new9.technicalIntricacy: A mixed number combines a whole-number count with a leftover proper fraction, both describing the same overall quantity together.
frac_l1_new9.realPurpose: Mixed numbers are the everyday way people describe quantities like '2 and three-quarters cups', making them easier to picture than an equivalent improper fraction.

variants.question: What is 1/4 of 20?
What is 3/5 of 25?
What is 2/3 of 18?

frac_l1_new10.technicalIntricacy: Finding a fraction of a quantity means dividing the quantity by the denominator (to find the value of one part) and then multiplying by the numerator (to find how many of those parts are needed).
frac_l1_new10.realPurpose: This calculation is used constantly in everyday situations, such as finding a discount, a portion of a recipe, or a share of a total amount.

variants.question: What is {{p}}/{{q}} + {{r}}/{{q}}, expressed as a single fraction (do not simplify)?

frac_l2_new3.technicalIntricacy: Adding fractions that already share a denominator only requires adding the numerators; the shared denominator itself never changes, since the size of the equal parts being counted stays the same.
frac_l2_new3.realPurpose: This is the essential first case of fraction addition, and it must be mastered before tackling fractions with unlike denominators.

variants.question: What is {{p}}/{{q}} − {{r}}/{{q}}, expressed as a single fraction (do not simplify)?

frac_l2_new4.technicalIntricacy: Subtracting fractions with the same denominator only requires subtracting the numerators, keeping the shared denominator fixed, since both fractions are already split into equally sized parts.
frac_l2_new4.realPurpose: This mirrors like-fraction addition and is essential for correctly finding the difference between two quantities measured in equal-sized parts, such as remaining ingredient amounts.

variants.question: What is {{p}}/{{q}} of {{whole}}?

frac_l2_new5.technicalIntricacy: Finding a fraction of a larger quantity means dividing that quantity by the denominator to get the value of one equal part, then multiplying by the numerator to get the required number of those parts.
frac_l2_new5.realPurpose: This is the general version of finding 'a fraction of a total', used whenever a share, discount, or portion of a larger real-world quantity must be calculated.

variants.question: A student solves 2/3 ÷ 4/5 by dividing the numerators and denominators directly (2 ÷ 4 and 3 ÷ 5), instead of multiplying by the reciprocal. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Dividing fractions is not done by dividing numerators and denominators separately; the correct method is to multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12, not the result of dividing numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator
distractors: The student's method is correct, since dividing fractions means dividing numerators and denominators directly
2/3 ÷ 4/5 should instead be found by adding the two fractions together
Fractions can only be divided if their denominators are already equal

frac_l3_new3.technicalIntricacy: Dividing by a fraction is defined as multiplying by its reciprocal; dividing the numerators and denominators term-by-term is not an equivalent operation and does not generally produce the same result.
frac_l3_new3.realPurpose: This is one of the most common fraction-division mistakes, and avoiding it is essential before correctly solving any real problem involving splitting a quantity into fractional portions.

variants.question: What is 3/4 written as a decimal?
What is 1/5 written as a decimal?
What is 0.6 written as a fraction in simplest form?

dec_l1_new3.technicalIntricacy: Converting a fraction to a decimal means dividing the numerator by the denominator, while converting a decimal back to a fraction means writing it over the matching place-value power of 10 and then simplifying.
dec_l1_new3.realPurpose: Being able to move fluently between fractions and decimals is essential since both forms appear constantly, from recipe measurements (fractions) to prices and readings (decimals).

variants.question: What is the place value of the digit 4 in 6.284?
What is the place value of the digit 2 in 6.284?
In expanded form, 5.36 is written as:

dec_l1_new4.technicalIntricacy: Decimal place values continue past the ones column into tenths, hundredths and thousandths, each ten times smaller than the last, and expanded form simply writes a decimal as the sum of each of these individual place values.
dec_l1_new4.realPurpose: Understanding place value beyond hundredths is necessary for reading precise scientific and financial figures that use three or more decimal places.

variants.question: Before adding two decimal numbers, what must you first do?
variants.answer: Line up the decimal points so each place value column matches
distractors: Round both numbers to the nearest whole number

variants.question: What is 4.5 + 2.3?
What is 7.6 − 3.2?

dec_l1_new5.technicalIntricacy: Lining up decimal points before adding or subtracting ensures each digit is combined only with digits of the exact same place value, just as whole-number columns are lined up by place value.
dec_l1_new5.realPurpose: This alignment step is used every time amounts of money, ingredients or measurements need to be combined or compared accurately.

variants.question: When multiplying 2.5 × 1.4, how many total decimal places should the answer have (before any simplifying)?
What is 0.3 × 0.2?
What is 1.5 × 2?

dec_l1_new6.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying decimals produces a result whose total decimal places equal the sum of the decimal places in each factor, which is why 0.3 × 0.2 (one decimal place each) gives 0.06, a two-decimal-place answer.
dec_l1_new6.realPurpose: This decimal-place rule lets you sanity-check a decimal multiplication answer's size and precision without needing to fully re-multiply the numbers.

variants.question: What is 6.4 ÷ 2?
What is 9.6 ÷ 4?
To divide a decimal by 10, you should move the decimal point:
distractors: Nowhere — decimals cannot be divided by 10

dec_l1_new7.technicalIntricacy: Dividing a decimal by a whole number splits its value into that many equal parts, while dividing specifically by a power of 10 shifts every digit's place value, moving the decimal point left by the matching number of places.
dec_l1_new7.realPurpose: Quick decimal division by 10, 100 or 1000 is used constantly for mental conversions, such as between rupees and paise, or metres and centimetres.

variants.question: Which is smaller in value: 0.500 or 0.6?
distractors: Cannot be determined without more digits

variants.question: Which is greater: 0.09 or 0.1?
Adding trailing zeros to the end of a decimal (changing 0.5 to 0.50) does what to its value?
variants.answer: Nothing — the value stays exactly the same

dec_l1_new8.technicalIntricacy: Trailing zeros written after the last non-zero decimal digit never change a decimal's value; comparing decimals correctly means comparing place value by place value, not simply counting how many digits each one has.
dec_l1_new8.realPurpose: Recognising that a shorter decimal isn't automatically smaller (and a longer one isn't automatically bigger) prevents a very common decimal-comparison mistake.

variants.question: What is 7.6 rounded to the nearest whole number?
What is 3.24 rounded to the nearest tenth?
What is 12.95 rounded to the nearest whole number?

dec_l1_new9.technicalIntricacy: Rounding to a given place depends only on the single digit immediately after that place: 5 or higher rounds the target digit up, and anything below 5 leaves it unchanged.
dec_l1_new9.realPurpose: Rounding to different levels of precision (whole numbers, tenths, hundredths) is used constantly depending on how precise a real-world measurement or amount needs to be.

variants.question: Between which two whole numbers does 5.7 lie on a number line?
Which decimal lies exactly halfway between 3 and 4 on a number line?
Which decimal lies exactly halfway between 0.2 and 0.4?

dec_l1_new10.technicalIntricacy: A decimal's whole-number part tells you which pair of whole numbers it sits between on a number line, and the midpoint between any two values is found by averaging them.
dec_l1_new10.realPurpose: Visualising decimals on a number line builds the same intuitive sense of size and position that is already familiar from whole numbers and integers.

dec_l2_new3.technicalIntricacy: Subtracting decimals requires the same decimal-point alignment as addition, matching each place value column before subtracting digit by digit.
dec_l2_new3.realPurpose: Decimal subtraction is used constantly for finding change due, remaining balances, or the difference between two measurements.

dec_l2_new4.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying two one-decimal-place numbers together produces a result with two decimal places in total, matching the sum of the decimal places in each factor.
dec_l2_new4.realPurpose: Multiplying two decimal quantities together is used whenever a rate or measurement (like a price per unit) must be scaled by another decimal quantity.

dec_l2_new5.technicalIntricacy: Dividing a decimal by a whole number splits its value into that many equal shares, keeping the same number of decimal places in the quotient as a clean division allows.
dec_l2_new5.realPurpose: This calculation is used whenever a decimal total (such as a length or a cost) must be split evenly across a fixed number of equal shares.

variants.question: A student multiplies 4.2 × 100 by simply writing two extra zeros at the end, getting 4.200 (read as 'four point two hundred'), instead of 420. What is the mistake?
variants.answer: Multiplying by 100 shifts every digit two place values to the left (moving the decimal point two places to the right), turning 4.2 into 420; simply appending zeros AFTER the decimal point (getting 4.200) doesn't move the decimal point at all, so the value stays completely unchanged (4.200 = 4.2, not 420)
distractors: The student's method is correct, since appending zeros after the decimal point always multiplies a number by 100
4.2 × 100 should equal 4.2 with two zeros placed immediately after the '4', giving 4002
Multiplying by 100 has no effect on a decimal number's value

dec_l3_new3.technicalIntricacy: Multiplying by a power of 10 moves the decimal point itself; trailing zeros written after the last non-zero decimal digit are a 'do-nothing' addition, since they never change a number's value regardless of how many are added.
dec_l3_new3.realPurpose: This distinction prevents a very common shortcut error, since visually 'adding zeros' looks similar whether it happens before or after the decimal point, even though the effect on value is completely different.

variants.question: A rational number is any number that can be written in the form p/q, where:
variants.answer: p and q are integers and q is not zero
distractors: p and q are whole numbers and p is not zero
p and q are both positive integers only
p and q are prime numbers

variants.question: Which of these is NOT automatically a rational number?
Is every integer also a rational number?
variants.answer: Yes — any integer n can be written as n/1
distractors: No, integers and rational numbers are unrelated
Only positive integers are rational numbers
Only zero is a rational number among integers

rat_l1_new1.technicalIntricacy: The definition p/q (with integer p and q, q ≠ 0) automatically includes every integer, whole number and natural number, since any of them can be written over a denominator of 1, while numbers like π cannot be written this way at all.
rat_l1_new1.realPurpose: Understanding exactly which numbers qualify as rational (and which, like π, do not) clarifies why rational numbers form a single broad system unifying integers and fractions.

variants.question: A rational number p/q is said to be in standard form when:
variants.answer: q is positive and p, q share no common factor other than 1 (in lowest terms)
distractors: p is always positive, regardless of q
p and q are both even numbers
q is always greater than p

variants.question: What is −6/8 written in standard form?
What is 5/−10 written in standard form?

rat_l1_new2.technicalIntricacy: Standard form requires both a positive denominator and full simplification, so a negative denominator must be rewritten with the negative sign moved to the numerator, and any common factor divided out.
rat_l1_new2.realPurpose: Standard form gives every rational number one single, unambiguous way to be written, which makes comparing and ordering rational numbers far more reliable.

variants.question: Where would you find the rational number −3/4 on a number line?
Where would you find the rational number 7/2 on a number line?

variants.question: Is the square of a negative number always positive, always negative, or does it depend on the number?

umv_l2_new2.questionTemplate: If {{litres1}} litres of petrol costs ₹{{cost1}}, what would {{litres2}} litres of the same petrol cost?
